Check this scene against the index and the scene card.

**Start with the computed evidence below.** The claim-by-claim comparison against canon is
assembled for you before you are called, so you do not have to recall what a file says: it
names every claim this draft makes, what canon holds for it, and whether that is a conflict,
a declared change, an agreement, or a first establishment. A finding about any of those
should quote from there. That block exists because the previous version of this brief told
you to read the index and the measured result was three shell reads across a nineteen-scene
run — and eleven findings whose contradicting side was an absence, because a model asked
what a file says without being shown it produces a plausible answer rather than a blank.

Then read what the comparison cannot settle. You have `bash` and `read` over the whole
project, and a finding that quotes the actual earlier scene is one the writer can act on
rather than argue with. Work through the five categories, using the files named:

**Factual detail** — appearance, names, counts, objects. Compare against
  `characters/<id>/profile.yaml` (identity, where a change is a retcon) and the
  earlier scenes under `novel/chapters/`. `grep -rn "<name>" novel/chapters/` finds
  every prior mention.
**Timeline and plot logic** — order, duration, simultaneity, cause. Compare against
  `events/timeline.jsonl` and the promise ledger `continuity/plot-contracts.jsonl`.
  This is ConStory's largest category and the easiest to miss by reading only the
  draft.
**Characterization** — motivation, ability, voice, and above all knowledge. Read
  `characters/<id>/beliefs.jsonl`: a character using something they have not learnt
  is the single most common defect in generated fiction, and it is invisible unless
  you check what they knew as of this scene.
**World building and setting** — rules, geography, technology. `world/rules.yaml`
  says what is true; it does not say who knows it. `locations/<id>.yaml` and prior
  scenes say what a place is like.
**Narrative style** — voice, tense, register drift. `novel/style/voice.md` and the
  previous scene are the comparison.

For a pair of characters, `read_relation_history` gives their history as narrative —
what they were to each other at each stage and what changed it. Reading the YAML
gives you the structure instead.

Report a defect with write_findings, one call per defect. Call nothing if it looks fine —
an empty finding list is a normal result and manufacturing a finding to appear useful
makes the novel worse.

Every finding needs a `suggestion`: what the writer should actually change. This is not
politeness, it is the difference between a defect that gets fixed and one that does not.
The writer has no shell, no index access and no way to look anything up — your finding is
the whole of what it knows about the problem. `make the timeline consistent` leaves it
guessing; `move the key's discovery to after Hale opens the door, and cut the later clause
claiming it was already in the lock` can be carried out. A scene that cannot be repaired
in the rounds available is committed with your finding attached to it, so a vague
suggestion becomes a permanent defect in the book rather than a lost round.

And use `canon_context` whenever the fix depends on a fact. You are the only participant
who can put one in front of the writer — it has no shell and no index — so a finding that
says a character cannot know something yet has to also say what they *do* know as of this
scene, quoted, with the file it came from. Without that the writer has two options and both
are bad: ignore you, or invent the fact. An invented fact reaches the page with nothing
anywhere recording that it was invented, which is the failure the whole index exists to
prevent. The same applies to a timeline, a distance, a name, a piece of history: quote it.

These are not defects:
  - metaphor, simile and figurative language are not factual claims
  - irony, sarcasm and understatement mean the opposite of their surface
  - an unreliable or limited narrator may state things the story contradicts on purpose
  - a character may lie, misremember or be mistaken; that is characterisation, not a defect
  - dream, hallucination, hypothetical and counterfactual passages do not assert fact
  - stream of consciousness may break grammar, tense and chronology deliberately
  - foreshadowing and deliberate withholding are not abandoned plot elements
  - a stated time may be approximate when a character is estimating
  - when a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, choose the literary one
When a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, take the literary one.

These subtypes can only ever be warnings at scene time, because at this point they are
not yet errors — an unpaid promise is an open loop until the story ends:
  causeless_effects, abandoned_plot_elements, skill_power_fluctuations, forgotten_abilities, social_norms_violations

For any contradiction you must quote both sides. If you cannot point at the passage it
contradicts, you have a suspicion, not a finding: report it as a warning or not at all.

An entity being absent from the packet does not mean it does not exist. The packet
carries state for the characters *present in this scene*; the full cast is in the
entity roster and on disk under characters/, locations/ and objects/. Check there
before reporting that something was invented — that mistake cost three attempts on a
scene whose entities were in the plan the whole time.

**An absence in the index is not a defect.** This is the direction that is easy to get
backwards, and getting it backwards is expensive. A scene is where facts are
established: the object with no `provenance` yet, the character whose profile records no
quotes yet, the pair with no relation history yet — those are all the normal state of an
index *before* this scene is folded in. index-manager writes them at commit, from this
prose. So `objects/obj-note.yaml has no first_seen entry` and `the relation query returns
nothing for these two` are not findings; they are what a first appearance looks like.

A finding needs a **conflict with something the index actually records**, and you must be
able to quote both sides. If one side of your pair is an empty file, a missing key, or a
query that returned nothing, you do not have a contradiction — you have a scene doing its
job. Report nothing.

Nor is an unmet request a *consistency* defect. The orchestrator's brief may ask for things
it invented on the spot; a draft that declines one is not contradicting the world, and no
subtype fits. Do not file that with `write_findings`.

The scene card is different, and the distinction matters now that there are two channels. A
card is the plan's account of what this scene is for, so a scene that does something else
belongs on the craft axis as `off_brief` — not because an instruction was disobeyed, but
because the task's own requirements are what the Relevance dimension is scored against. A
brief invented mid-run is not; if the two disagree, the card wins.

Why this is stated so heavily: a run where the verifier raised eleven findings of this
shape scored *worse* than one that raised five real ones. The writer cannot tell a
spurious finding from a real one — it has no shell and no index — so it spends its repair
rounds adding provenance sentences to prose that was fine, and the prose is what is
scored.

You can read the whole book. `run_command` reaches every committed scene under
novel/chapters/, every character file, the relation records and the promise ledger — so
when a passage looks wrong, check before reporting. The packet is what the writer was
given, not the limit of what you may consult, and a finding that quotes the actual
earlier scene is one the writer can act on rather than argue with.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

So report those with `write_craft_finding`. The checks, each naming the scored dimension
that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Relevance — "content highly relevant and fully applicable to the user's request"; LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment — "how effectively the story meets the readers' expectations based on the premise and genres"
- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. Not the same words — the same content: a suspicion re-voiced, a relationship re-explained, a clue re-found. This is what makes a long story feel padded rather than long, and verbatim overlap does not detect it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth — "seriously lacking breadth and depth with minimal information"; LongBench-Write Reading Experience — "boring and hard to understand"
- **nothing_changes** (can block) — the situation at the end of the scene is the situation at the start. Nobody knows something new, owes something new, has lost something or has decided. Name the state at the open and the state at the close; if you cannot name a difference, that is the finding.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Coherence — "disorganized structure with no coherence"; LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **internal_incoherence** (can block) — the scene contradicts itself, with both halves inside this draft — a detail stated one way early and another way late, a character reacting to something they have not been told in this scene, a sequence that cannot have happened in the order given. This needs no index at all, which is why it is inexcusable to miss.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy — "content with numerous errors and highly misleading"; LongBench-Write Coherence
- **summary_not_scene** (warning only) — events reported rather than dramatised — a paragraph that says an argument happened instead of letting it happen. Compression is legitimate and necessary; a scene whose central beat is summarised is not compressed, it is skipped.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Writing and Language — "the writing style's ability to engage and captivate readers"
- **thin_for_its_length** (warning only) — the scene is near its word target and carries one beat's worth of content, padded with restatement, weather, or interiority that repeats itself. The grader penalises this and the length score does not reward it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **costless_conflict** (warning only) — a conflict resolved without costing anybody anything specific. Partial and temporary resolutions are fine; free ones read as unearned.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Emotional Impact — "the story's ability to evoke strong and deep emotional impact"
- **theme_stated** (warning only) — a sentence that explains what the story means, rather than a choice that tests it. Quote the sentence — it is almost always removable without loss.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Themes — "how well the themes are explored throughout the story"
- **flat_diction** (warning only) — constructions repeating within the scene, filter verbs standing in for perception ("she felt that", "he realised that"), abstraction where a concrete detail belongs, or sentence rhythm that does not move with the tension.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Writing and Language; LongBench-Write Clarity — "confusing expression with minimal details"
- **inert_open_or_close** (warning only) — the scene opens on setting or mood rather than a situation already in motion, or closes on a mood rather than a specific next beat — an unanswered question, a door about to open. In a long story this is what decides whether the reader turns over.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Enjoyment and Engagement
- **genre_promise_unmet** (warning only) — the scene declines the obligation its genre carries — a horror scene with nothing at stake, a romance scene with no charge between the two people, a mystery scene that advances no inference. Breaking a genre promise deliberately is legitimate; it has to be visibly deliberate.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment; LongBench-Write Relevance

Two rules, both enforced by the tool rather than left to your judgement:

Only these may be **error** and therefore cost the writer a round: off_brief, restates_prior_scene, nothing_changes, internal_incoherence, ending_not_delivered.
Everything else is a warning — it reaches the writer and costs nothing. That asymmetry is
deliberate: a craft judgement a reader could reasonably disagree with must not be able to
hold up a scene.

And a blocking craft finding needs **checkable evidence**, in the shape the check names.
Either two verbatim quotes (this draft, and the earlier passage it repeats or the half of
itself it contradicts), or a named state pair — what is true when the scene opens and what
is true when it closes. `nothing_changes` is precisely the claim that you cannot name a
difference, so name both halves and let the pair be the evidence. If you cannot produce
the evidence, you have an impression: report it as a warning, which is a perfectly useful
thing to do.

`suggestion` is mandatory on every craft finding, warnings included. The writer cannot see
the manuscript, the index or the rubric. A craft note without an instruction is a complaint
it can only answer by guessing, and a guessed craft repair damages prose that was working —
which is not hypothetical: a run whose findings the writer could not act on scored 8.4
points below one with fewer, better ones.

At most two craft findings can block one round, whatever you report. Consistency comes
first when both are present: it is counted by name and craft is not. So if you have three
craft blockers, the third is a warning — pick the two that most damage the scene.

## What the orchestrator asked for on this scene

Review draft s-001 for consistency with world rules and craft. Check: scene names the Academy's annual intake (one hundred) and the ten-year three-leave statistic; establishes Rue sold herself and signed the Contract with a ten-year term; mentions Folio and Bell. Verify no contradictions. Note craft issues: voice, length (target ~1176 words, current 1018), if missing details (e.g., exact legal wording of Contract) then mark as a finding but not a blocker unless it creates a world-rule contradiction. Provide an audit file with line-referenced findings. Approve if only craft notes and length shortfall; allow one repair round. Reply with verdict and audit path.

That is in addition to your standing instructions above, not instead of them.
If it states a story fact that is not in your packet — a name, a measurement, a
quotation, a piece of history — that fact has not been checked against the index by
anyone. Ask about it or establish it yourself in the state delta. Do not write it down
as though it were already true.

## P0

### scene-card  <novel/chapters/ch-01/chapter.yaml>

Scene s-001. Intent: Prologue: Rue, in poverty, makes the conscious choice to sell herself to the Mercy Academy. We see the private, practical reasons for her decision, the signing of the Contract, and the Ceremony Hall's polished charity. Establish Rue's voice and the moment of consent.
Present: char-rue, loc-ceremony-hall, obj-contract, obj-folio, char-headmistress, group-the-hundred, loc-mercy-academy
Target length: about 1176 words.

### logline  <novel/outline/logline.md>

Rue sold herself into the Mercy Academy, an institution that takes one hundred girls a year and returns almost none; decades later, as a war rolls up to the Academy's gates, Rue must face what binding herself to the Academy cost her and whether the bargains written in its folios can — or should — be broken.

### entity-roster  <characters/, locations/, objects/>

Every entity that exists in this story. Only these ids may be used; if you need someone or something that is not here, say so rather than inventing an id.
- char-rue: Rue: the protagonist. Sold herself into the Mercy Academy as a young woman. She spends decades inside and ages there; resolute, observant, versed in the Academy's rituals and archives.
- group-the-hundred: The Hundred: the yearly cohort of girls the Academy takes into its care. An institutional number, a social body with shifting members and shared customs.
- group-the-three: The Three: the rare survivors who leave the Academy after its ten-year term. They are a myth, a statistic, and a tangible but infrequent occurrence.
- char-headmistress: Headmistress: the Academy's senior administrator and public face — formal, composed, expert at maintaining the Academy's charitable image and its internal discipline.
- char-war-envoy: War Envoy: an emissary and later manifestation of the approaching war — part diplomat, part herald of force — who arrives at the Academy's gates during Rue's later years.
- loc-mercy-academy: Mercy Academy: the institution itself — a walled compound of dormitories, classrooms, a ceremony hall, gardens, an archive and a sealed ledger room. Known outwardly as a benevolent house of care.
- loc-ceremony-hall: Ceremony Hall: the Academy's public-facing space where intakes, pledge-signings, and public audiences with the Headmistress occur.
- loc-dormitory: Dormitory: where the Hundred sleep and keep their limited possessions; a place of whispered alliances, small rebellions and nightly reckonings.
- loc-archive: Archive: the Academy's records room, holding intake folios, contracts, and the private ledger that traces each girl's status and fate.
- loc-garden: Garden: a carefully tended courtyard inside Academy walls. The place where girls are allowed to gather, work, and speak more freely — and where Rue does much of her thinking.
- loc-gates: Gates: the Academy's outer gate and the road beyond. The point at which the war and its emissaries first make contact with the Academy.
- obj-contract: Contract: the binding document girls sign (or the Academy signs for them) on intake. It defines the ten-year term and the Academy's claims; for Rue it is the instrument she once sold herself to.
- obj-folio: Folio: the intake ledger used in Ceremony Hall. It records names, provenance, dates, and occasionally marginal notes that tell of exceptions — where The Three are noted, or where a girl vanishes.
- obj-bell: Bell: a bronze bell in the courtyard rung at set times — intake, curfew, alarms. Its single clear note marks the Academy's rhythms and the day the war arrives.

### world-rules  <world/rules.yaml>

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- Every year, the Mercy Academy acquires exactly one hundred girls; that number is an institutional constant and must appear in the story's facts.
- After a ten-year period within the Academy, only three individuals ever leave under normal circumstances; this must be stated and preserved as a factual statistic within the narrative.
- Rue entered the Mercy Academy by selling herself; her consent and the Contract she signed must be an established fact in her backstory.
- A war arrives and reaches the Academy's gates during Rue's later years; the war must affect events at the Academy and force reckonings with its past.
- The Folio and the Contract are authoritative objects inside the Academy: they record intake and the terms of binding. Any scene that refers to who is allowed to leave must trace to these artifacts or to a documented exception.
- Do not contradict the above institutional facts anywhere in the story; if new facts about the Academy's practices are introduced, they must be consistent with the above constraints or be revealed as covert exceptions with provenance in the Archive.

## The draft

I arrived with my pockets full of nothing and the honest calculation that followed. Two coins would stretch two days at the market; one bed at the lodging house meant a back that never stopped aching and a mouth that never stopped asking. There are neat words for bravery and grander sentences for sacrifice. I had twenty years' worth of sentences inside me. What I had in the moment was hunger and arithmetic. So I sold myself.

The Ceremony Hall smelled of beeswax polish and boiled linen: the kind of clean that announces itself rather than earning quiet trust. Light came through high windows in long, patient bars. The hundred benches were arranged like a small amphitheatre; families sat in the outer rings, sober as undertakers. In the middle, on a low table, lay the Folio and the Contract: the Folio a wide, dark book with a ribbon that had once been more important than it was now; the Contract folded into a small, precise packet, the paper rubbed where hands had touched it for decades.

The Folio was open where a scribe had left it, a pale rectangle of invitation: “Folio Entry — Name: __________________; Age: __; Date: ______; Intake: One hundred; Provenance (sold/placed/orphaned): __________; Signature: __________________; Witness: Headmistress / Scribe.” I read it while they adjusted the sash at the back of my shirt. Reading paperwork is a kind of prayer for people like me.

They called the intake. The Bell — a single bronze note struck from a high arch — cut the murmurs and put us under the House's attention. I counted the sound more as an accountant than a believer: one clear note for the beginning, then the low chorus of the Headmistress's voice as she took the liturgy of charity down the line.

The Headmistress was everything polished with use. She wore mercy as other people wear good coats — tailored to fit, and kept for public weather. Her voice carried over the benches in a soft, precise tide. She read the facts aloud in the way a town clerk reads a deed.

"Out of the hundred who enter each year," she said, "only three leave at the end of their ten-year term. The rest remain under the Academy's charge as is recorded." There was no scolding there, only the small hardness of a truth stated so the room could register it. I had expected myth; I had not expected arithmetic.

When she closed, she laid the policy of the House into a sentence that would follow all our names, and repeated the line that the Folio itself required be heard: "So entered under the charge of the Mercy Academy. Let the Folio stand as record and law. Let those within this house remember that mercy is accounted for by service and attention, not by indulgence." The scribe moved an inkwell with ceremonious care, and the Contract was handed to me.

There are ways to refuse that sound like refusal and ways that are simple. I did not make a show of hesitating. I thought of the lodging house's thin broth, the cough from the woman who shared my bed, the child who asked for a scrap she would not get. I thought of work under a roof that would not change its mind because a winter came early.

The Contract's clause was quiet in the packet but not shy: ten years. The writing named it without flourish — a span not measured in noble phrase but in the clear currency of years. I traced the number with a fingertip as the scribe held the folio steady. Ten years is a ledger entry; it is not a promise of comfort.

I signed in a hand that had practised keeping accounts in cramped ledgers. The pen felt like a small instrument of business. My name was a line, small and tidy. The scribe copied it into the Folio in ink that smelled of iron and permanence. The Headmistress dipped a fingertip and made a mark beside the signature — her witness. The page closed.

There was applause, the kind meant to be mindful. A girl near me cried once, sharp and immediate; nobody shushed her. Mourning and commerce live in the same house and know how to move around one another.

Outside the Hall the sun hit the Academy walls. Inside, the Folio rested where it would be put to the Archive later, an obvious book that contained, in its margins, the small remarks that always get made: nicknames, a note if someone arrived with a child, exceptions the institution had allowed itself. I had read enough of such margins to know that there are things only the Archive says aloud, and only later.

I walked out with a small packet in my palm and a larger accounting on my shoulders. The bargain I had made was practical and unsentimental: room, work, a roof, and ten years of measured claims. The Academy had the language for it all — intake, witness, folio, charge — and I had my signature. I had consented.

Later I would learn the ways the house keeps its numbers neat: how the Folio is consulted when a girl asks to leave, how the ledger rooms hold answer-keys to questions you do not yet have. For now, the decision that mattered was simple and cold as coin: I had fewer options than the day before and one guaranteed where-to-sleep. My humor about it was small and private. I told myself the trade was sensible.

When the bronze note sounded again, it sounded like a clock. The Bell finished the ceremony and put the House back into its ordinary rhythm. I folded the Contract into my pocket the way you fold a receipt for a transaction that you do not plan to return. That night, when I lay in my clean bed for the first time in months, I thought of the Folio's blank lines and the Headmistress's closing line, and I felt the arithmetic of my choice settle down into the room: a tidy sum, a term, and a witness.

What I checked (high level)

Findings (audit)
1) Craft — thin_for_its_length (warning)
- Offending passage (verbatim, from s-001 draft):
  "There are ways to refuse that sound like refusal and ways that are simple. I did not make a show of hesitating. I thought of the lodging house's thin broth, the cough from the woman who shared my bed, the child who asked for a scrap she would not get."

The draft is 1018 words against a 1176 target and the shortfall manifests as summarisation of core beats rather than dramatization.

For example, expand the signing into a short moment: show the scribe sliding the pen, the scribe asking one brief question ("Do you accept these terms?"), Rue's thumb tracing the "ten years" in the packet, a visible tremor in her hand, the Headmistress's small, appraising look, and the single girl's cry lingering as Rue signs. Alternatively, dramatize Rue's internal calculation with a concrete sensory image (the lodging-house woman's cough filling the threshold of her attention) so consent reads as costly and witnessed.
- Severity: warning (not blocking).
- Where to change: the signing/decision paragraphs in scene s-001 (the section around "I did not make a show of hesitating." through "I had consented."). The quoted passage in the finding points to the exact place to expand.
